en: Continued Record of the Transmission of the Lamp, Volume One.
Under the First Great Mirror (Dajian), Tenth Generation:
Dharma Heirs of Chan Master Shoushan Nian. Dharma Heirs of Chan Master Shoushan Nian.
Chan Master Shanzhao of Fenyang Taiziyuan was a native of the Yu clan of Taiyuan. His character and insight were profound and far-reaching;
from his youth, he was free from artificiality and possessed great wisdom.
He naturally mastered all scripts and characters without relying on a teacher's instruction.
At the age of fourteen, his parents passed away one after the other;
left alone and suffering, he grew weary of worldly toil and defilement.
Having shaved his head and received full ordination,
he traveled on foot to various regions, staying in each place for only a short time;
he took no pleasure in sightseeing.
He visited various masters throughout the land at random, studying under seventy-one teachers of the Dharma.
Finally, he arrived at Shoushan.
One day, Shoushan ascended the seat.
The Master stepped forward and asked,
"What is the meaning behind Baizhang rolling up his mat?"
Shan said, "The dragon’s sleeve sweeps it open, and the whole body is fully manifest.
[The other] asked, "What is your meaning, Master?"
Shan said, "Where the Elephant King walks, there are no fox tracks.
At these words, the Master attained great enlightenment; bowing and rising, he said:
"The moon in the empty expanse over the ten-thousand-year-old emerald pool—
only after repeatedly searching and grasping will one finally come to know it. Someone asked:
"What principle did you perceive that you were so readily convinced?
The Master replied,
"This is precisely where I have surrendered my body and life."
Later, he traveled through the regions of Heng, Xiang, and Xiangyang.
Each time local magistrates earnestly invited him to renowned monasteries, they did so as many as eight times;
yet he remained firm in his reclining posture and did not respond.
Upon the passing of Shoushan,
the monastics and laypeople of the western regions dispatched the monk Qichong to invite him to serve as abbot; however,
the Master remained behind his closed door with his head resting high upon his pillow.
Cong pushed open the door and entered, remonstrating with him, saying:
"The Great Matter of the Buddha-dharma requires one to set aside minor details.
Fengxue feared that he would fulfill the prophecy [of his own demise] and that the essential tenets of our school would fall into ruin."
Fortunately, there was my former teacher.
My former teacher has already passed away.
You are one who possesses the strength to shoulder the Great Dharma of the Tathāgata.
"What time is it now that you wish to sleep peacefully?
The Master started in alarm, rose, and grasping Cōng’s hand,
said, "If it were not for you, I would never have heard such words."
Having prepared for his final journey,
he sat in meditation upon a single mat;
for thirty years, his feet did not cross the threshold.
Both monastics and laypeople alike called him Fenyang and did not dare address him by name.
Entering the hall, he said to the assembly:
"In the gate of Fenyang, there dwells a Lion of West River, crouching right before the entrance."
Whoever comes here is immediately bitten to death.
What skillful means (*upāya*) is there for entering the gate of Fenyang and seeing the person of Fenyang?
If one were to see the person of Fenyang...
He was capable of serving as a teacher to the patriarchs and Buddhas.
Have you not seen that everyone at Fenyang was a man who died standing on the spot?
Is there anyone today who can enter [this state] as well?
Enter quickly so as not to let your lifelong efforts go to waste.
If you are not a guest of the Dragon Gate, take care not to suffer the "dotted forehead.
Which one is a guest of the Dragon Gate? Point them all out at once!
Raising his staff, he said:
"Withdraw quickly, withdraw quickly; take care!
He then ascended the hall and said:
Every single phrase must possess the three mysteries (san xuán mén), and each mystery must possess the three essentials (yī xuán mén xū jù sān yào).
Which phrase is this "three mysteries and three essentials"?
Quickly try to understand it!
Each of you should reflect for yourselves:
have you yet attained a state of stability?
The ancients of old traveled on foot as pilgrims.
If you have heard a single karmic condition but have not yet clarified it within yourself, you will immediately find no flavor in food and drink and find no peace in sleep or rest.
You must resolve this with urgency; do not treat it as a minor matter.
This is why the Elder of Great Enlightenment appeared in the world for the sake of the one great matter.

Consider this: from the time of our predecessors until now, those who have traveled on foot have not done so to tour mountains, play by the water, or gaze upon the splendors of prefectures and capitals.
Wearing but a single robe and subsisting on food received by mouth were both because his sacred mind had not yet attained full penetration;
therefore, he traveled far and wide on foot,
resolving profound mysteries and proclaiming them far and wide.
One extensively seeks out those with prior realization and draws near to those of high virtue;
this is for the purpose of continuing the lamp of the Buddha’s mind, perpetuating the ancestral lineage,
exalting the holy seed, and guiding future practitioners.
This is for the benefit of oneself and others.
Is there anyone present now who wishes to deliberate?
If there is, come forward and let us deliberate together.
A monk asked,
"What is the phrase for receiving a beginner?
The Master said:
"You are a wandering monk.
[The monk] asked, "What is the phrase that distinguishes a patch-robed monk?
The Master said:
In the West, the sun rises in the hour of Mao.
[The student] asked, "What is the phrase for when the true command is being enacted?
The Master said:
Lichi came forward and presented his usual countenance,
asking, "What is the phrase that establishes heaven and earth?
The Master said:
In the continent of Uttarakuru, there is long-grained non-glutinous rice;
those who eat it experience neither anger nor joy.
Thus it is said:
These four turning words are used to test the monks of the world;
as soon as you come forward, they have already been tested.
[The Master] asked: "What is the place where a student exerts effort?"
The Master said,
"Striking the Great Image at Jiazhou.
[The student] asked, "What is the place where the student turns?"
The Master said,
"Guan Tie-niu of Shanfu. [The monk] asked,
"What is the point of intimacy for a student?"
The Master said:
"Xihe plays with the lion," and then he spoke.
If a person has mastered these three phrases and resolved the Three Mysteries,
there remain further words of the Three Essentials that must be thoroughly realized.
This was not chanted for the masses as a mere commonplace matter:
"The Three Mysteries and Three Essentials are difficult to distinguish;
when one attains the meaning and forgets the words, the Way is easy to approach."
A single phrase clearly encompasses the myriad phenomena.
On the Double Ninth, the chrysanthemums are fresh.
Because the weather in Bingfen was bitterly cold, the Master canceled the night assembly.
A certain bhikṣu arrived, shaking his mendicant’s staff,
and said to the Master:
"In this assembly there are six great beings."
"Why do you not preach the Dharma?
Having said this, he departed.
The Master secretly recorded this in a verse:
The Hu monk Jinguang came to Fenyang for the sake of the Dharma;
six men became great vessels.
I exhort you to propagate this widely.
When ascending the hall, every single word must embody the three mysteries (san-hsüan);
each mystery, in turn, must embody the three essentials (san-yao).
There is both illumination and function;
sometimes illumination precedes function,
and sometimes function precedes illumination.
Either illumination and function are simultaneous,
or illumination and function are not simultaneous—
first illuminating and subsequently functioning.
Furthermore, I wish to deliberate with you:
first employ it, then reflect upon it;
you must indeed be a person of substance for this to succeed.
If illumination and function are simultaneous, how do you respond?
If illumination and function are not simultaneous—
How, then, do you integrate yourself with it?
A monk asked:
"What is the source of the Great Way?"
The Master said,
"Digging in the earth to seek the heavens.
[The monk] asked, "How can it be like this?"
The Master said,
"You do not understand the profound mystery.
[The student] asked, "What is the guest within the guest?"
The Master said:
"With palms joined before the hermitage, ask the World-Honored One:
'What is the host within the guest?'"
The Master said,
"Facing each other, there is no companion.
[The student] asked, "What is the guest within the host?"
The Master said:
"Clouds of battle stretch across the sea;
drawing the sword, he stirs the Dragon Gate."
He asked, "What is the master among masters?
The Master said,
"Three heads and six arms, supporting heaven and earth."
The wrathful Nātha strikes the imperial bell.
Entering the hall: Fenyang has three secrets;
it is difficult for patch-robed monks to discern them.
He was about to ask how it was when [the Master] drove his staff straight into the monk's head.
At that time, a monk asked:
"What are these three secrets?
The Master struck him.
The monk bowed.
The Master said:
"I shall provide you with a verse for each at once;
this is the first secret instruction."
There is no time for guidance;
skillful words cannot describe it.
It is like the moon in the blue sky when the clouds part.
The second secret instruction:
Radiating light to discern the worthy and wise;
engaging in dialogue with a mind that benefits sentient beings.
The third secret instruction: to pull out the wedge from the eye,
as spoken by the barbarian masters of the Western Regions.
The Ji River flows through Silla.
In the northern regions, they use bing-iron.
Again he said:
Is there anyone who understands?
If there is one who understands, come forth and deliver a message;
I wish to know the extent of your realization.
Do not merely memorize words and phrases as if they were the entirety of your life; what benefit is there in that? There is none.
Do not stand for long; take care.
A monk asked,
"What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
The Master said:
A fan of blue silk provides sufficient breeze and coolness.
When asked about the cloth drum,
it hangs before the window.
"Who is the one who understands?
The Master said:
"Setting down the hoe and pouring out the wheat porridge."
Lying on the grass, he did not raise his head.
When asked, "What is the site of enlightenment?
the Master said:
It is not permitted to cast it down.
[A monk] asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
The Master said:
"Thoroughly to the bone and thoroughly to the marrow.
[The student] asked, "What is the meaning of this?
[The Master] said, "Pervading heaven and pervading earth."
Question: "A person who truly cultivates the Way does not see the faults of the world.
I do not yet understand what kind of faults they do not see.
The Master said:
The snow buries the night moon three feet deep;
a boat travels upon dry land for ten thousand li.
[The monk] asked, "What kind of mental activity is this, Master?"
The Master said,
"It is rather your own mental activity.
[The monk] asked, "What is the house style of the Master?"
The Master said:
"The Three Mysteries open the Way;
a single phrase shatters heterodox schools."
A monk asked, "What is the master’s livelihood?
The Master said,
"I do not grasp anything in my hands as is usual."
He made offerings to the monks of the Five Lakes and asked, "I wonder what they eat?
The Master said:
"Divine *sudhā* rice is no rare delicacy;
with a single taste of fine soup, one is satisfied and rests.
Entering the hall, he said to the assembly:
Now, one who expounds the Dharma must possess the ten wisdoms that accord with reality.
If one does not possess these ten wisdoms that accord with reality,
one cannot distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox, nor differentiate between the monastic and the lay.
Unable to serve as eyes for humans and devas to discern right from wrong,
he was like a bird flying through the sky with broken wings,
or like an arrow shot at a target with its string severed.
Because the bowstring is broken, the arrow does not hit the mark;
because the feathers are shattered, the arrow cannot fly through the air.
When the string is strong and the feathers are firm, the arrow pierces through both the air and the target.
"What is meant by 'the ten wisdoms being identical with reality'?
Let me point them out for you, venerable elders:
first, identity of substance."
Second, sharing the same great task;
third, collectively participating in the study;
fourth, sharing the same true wisdom.
Fifth, they are identical in pervasiveness;
sixth, they are identical in being fully endowed;
seventh, they are identical in gain and loss.
Eighth, they share the same birth and death;
ninth, they share the same sound in their roar;
tenth, they share the same entry [into realization].
It is further asked:
"With what kind of person does one enter together?
With whom does one roar with the same voice?"
How is it that there is a shared birth and death?
What thing is shared in gain and loss?
Which one is fully possessed in common?
What is this universal pervasiveness?
Who shares in true wisdom?
Who is able to participate in this total harmony?
Which one is the same as the Great Matter?
What thing is of the same substance?
Is there anyone who can bring it forth?
Those who can point it out do not begrudge their compassion;
those who cannot point it out have yet to possess the eye of study.
You must discern this with all earnestness.
To recognize right and wrong, one must see their true face in the present; it cannot be otherwise.
I have stood here long; take care.
Lord Li, the Governor of Longde Prefecture, has been an old friend of the Master.
Xu sent him to Tiansi Temple.
Although the messenger went three times, he did not respond.
When the messenger was punished and returned, he said:
“If you must have me as your teacher, we shall go together;
otherwise, there is nothing for it but death.
The Master laughed and said:
"I am already old and ill, so I shall not leave the mountain. You may go ahead;
we need not depart together."
The messenger said,
"If you agree, Master, then let me choose whether you go first or last.
The Master then ordered that a meal be prepared and his travel gear be readied.
He addressed the assembly, saying, "The old monk is departing; who can follow me?
A monk stepped forward and said:
"Such-and-such a person obtained it accordingly.
The Master asked,
"How many li do you travel each day?"
The monk said,
"Fifty li. The Master said:
"You cannot follow me," he said.
Then another monk came forward and said,
"I can follow him."
The Master asked,
"How many li do you travel each day?
The monk said:
After seventy li,
the Master said, "You cannot follow me."
The attendant stepped forward and said,
"I shall receive it accordingly."
"But wherever the Master goes, I shall go there as well.
The Master said,
"In that case, you have indeed followed me, old monk."
Having finished speaking, he said to the messenger,
"I shall go on ahead first," and he passed away while his chopsticks remained suspended.
The attendant immediately established the funeral pyre for cremation, collected the *śarīra*, and erected a stupa.

Chan Master Guisong of Guangjiao Monastery in Ye County, Ru Prefecture, was the son of the Jia family of Ji Prefecture; he entered the monastic order and received full ordination at Baoshou Monastery in Yi Prefecture when he reached the age of twenty.
Later, he traveled to visit Shoushan.
One day, Shoushan held up a bamboo stick and asked, "To call it a 'bamboo stick' is to encounter resistance; not to call it a 'bamboo stick' is to turn one's back."
"What do you call this?
The Master picked it up, threw it onto the ground, and said, "What is this?"
Shan said, "Blind.
At these words, the Master attained sudden and thorough enlightenment.
When he opened the hall for teaching, a monk asked:
"From patriarch to patriarch, the patriarchal seal has been transmitted.
Whom do you, Master, now take as your Dharma heir?
The Master replied:
"The Son of Heaven within the realm, the General beyond the frontier.
[The questioner] says: "It is like a drop in the ocean; I have received the Master's pointing-out.
As for the matter of the Supreme Vehicle (zōngshèng) that transcends this, what is it?"
The Master said:
"Before the Hall of the High Ancestor, Fan Kuai was enraged;
one must know that ten thousand *li* away, smoke and dust are utterly absent."
Question: "The chamber of Vimalakīrti does not take the sun and moon as its illumination.
What serves as the illumination for the Master’s chamber?
The Master said:
His eyebrows were parted in the shape of the character "八" (eight).
[The monk] asked, "I do not yet understand the meaning of this;
how is it? The Master said:
His two ears hung down past his shoulders.
[The monk] asked, "What is it that transcends the master?
The Master said:
"How long are the old monk’s eyebrows?
[The questioner asked. "What is the body revealed alone amidst the dust?
The Master said:
"A thousand-person tent in the north of the Great Wall;
ten-thousand-hu capacity boat in the south of the Yangtze River.
[The Master said: "If it is thus, then it is not dust."
The Master said:
"For those who merely parrot words, a single sheet of paper contains ten thousand practices.
[A student] asked: "What is the Master’s profound depth?"
The Master said:
"The cat has the merit of drinking blood;
the tiger has the virtue of raising the dead."
[The monk] said, "Is it not simply that there is nothing?
The Master said, "The pestle pounds in the southeast; the millstone grinds in the northwest."
Question: "What is the indestructible vajra body?
The Master said:
"Reduced to a hundred fragments."
He asked, "What is the meaning?
The Master said,
"In the end, it is but a heap of ashes."
Question: "It does not fall into any conditions;
please, Master, speak directly.
The Master said: "It falls."
Question: "What is the pure Dharma-body?
The Master said:
"A bamboo tally at the head of a latrine."
Question: What are precept, concentration, and wisdom?
The Master said:
"The implements for breaking things."
One day the Master ascended the seat.
A monk asked,
"What is it like when one has just come up into the Dharma Hall?"
The Master struck the meditation seat once.
The monk asked,
"I do not yet understand what this meaning is."
The Master said,
"No one has offered more than three hundred coins, so I shall sell it for that price.
He asked, "If a person of great *icchantika* nature were to come along, would you still act for his sake?"
The Master said,
"When the Dharma has long endured, it becomes corrupt.
[The monk] asked, "Wherein lies its compassion?"
The Master said,
"In old age, one becomes a demon. He then ascended the hall for formal instruction.
Whether ordinary or sagely, the bloodline of the patriarchs includes Nāgārjuna and Aśvaghoṣa,
as well as the cauldrons and furnaces of heaven and hell, and the Ox-Headed Hell-Warden.
The myriad phenomena of the universe— the sun, moon, and stars;
sentient and insentient beings of this world and other realms—
with his hand, he drew a single stroke and said:
Both enter this school.
Within this school, one can both kill people and bring them to life.
To kill a person, one must obtain the sword for killing.
To save a person, one must possess the phrase that saves a person.
What is the sword that kills and the phrase that saves?
If anyone can speak it, come forth and speak it before the assembly.
"If you cannot say it, you will have wasted your entire life. Take care.
He asked, "What is the Master’s four immeasurable minds?"
The Master said,
"Setting fire and killing people.
[The monk] asked, "Wherein lies compassion?"
The Master said:
"When you meet an enlightened person, present this to them.
[The student] asked: "It is not within, it is not without, and it is not in between."
"I do not know where it is," [the student] asked.
The Master said,
"Six in the Southern Dipper, seven in the Northern Dipper."
Question: "What is the Dharmakāya Lord Vairocana?
The Master said:
"The monastics are ranked by their years since ordination; the laity are ranked by their age."
[The student] asked, "Is there anything further above this?
The Master said, "There is.
[The student] asked, "What is the matter further above this?"
The Master said:
"Ten thousand li to Yuzhou—you go yourself;
as you depart, why do you feel such sorrow and resentment toward others?"
After sitting in the hall for a long while, he said:
"Now, those who travel as dhyāna practitioners must truly reflect upon themselves.
To study the Way, one must possess the eye of a student."
The ground of seeing must attain the phrase of the ground of seeing;
only then will there be a mutual affinity,
whereby one is no longer deluded by various sensory objects.
Nor does one fall into the evil realms.
Ultimately, how can this be fully understood?
At times, the words reach the mind, but the meaning does not.
Forgetting the external objects that serve as conditions, one discriminates among reflected images.
At times, the mind reaches the meaning while the words do not;
it is like the blind men feeling an elephant, each asserting a different version.
At times, both mind and words reach their limit,
shattering the realm of empty space;
its radiance illuminates the ten directions.
Sometimes both mind and words fail to reach it;
like a blind person wandering aimlessly back and forth,
they suddenly and without awareness fall into a deep pit.
Question: "What is the path that has been no different from ancient times to the present?
The Master said:
"Ordinary people all wrap their heads."
[The monk] asked, "What is the meaning?
The Master said,
"Dharma brother, you have no scholar's cap."
Question: "If one's own matter is not yet clear, what serves as the verification?
The Master said:
"Striking the signal gong for silence in the midst of a bustling marketplace."
[The questioner] asked, "What is the meaning?
The Master said,
"At noon, lighting the golden lamp."
Question: "When a cloth drum is struck in front of the hall, who is the one who understands?
The Master said:
"There is a rusty nail in your eye."
[The questioner] said, "I have not yet understood the meaning of this;
how is it so? The Master said, "Old Qiao competes with the Southern God."
A monk requested further instruction on the story of the "cypress tree.
The Master said,
"I shall not decline to explain it to you, but will you believe me?"
He replied, "The Master’s words are so weighty; how would I dare not believe them?
The Master said, "Do you hear the sound of water dripping from the eaves?"
The monk was suddenly enlightened; unconsciously, he let out a cry of "Aha!
The Master asked, "What principle have you seen?"
The monk then replied with a verse:
"Drops of water falling from the eaves,
distinct and clearly manifest."
He shattered heaven and earth;
in that very moment, his mind was stilled.
The Master then rejoiced.
He asked the monk, "At dusk you cast yourself into the forest; where did you depart from this morning?
The monk replied, "I am a newly ordained monk who has never studied Chan."
The Master said, "He entered hell in his living body; he has gone down there.
Later, a monk brought this up to Zen Master Zhimen Kuan.
Zhimen said:
"Why do you not say that the key is in the Master's hand?
Thereupon, the Master went to the infirmary to visit a sick monk. The monk asked:
The Master said, "The four elements of the monk's body are originally empty; from where does illness come?
The teacher replied, "It comes from the place where you, O Acharya, ask."
The monk, panting for breath, asked again:
"What is it like when there is no questioning?
The Master said:
"Letting go of the hand, he lies in the vast expanse.
The monk said, "Hey!
and immediately cast off his body.
Chan Master Shending Hongyin of Tanzhou was the son of the Hu family of Xiangshui.
Having set out on his travels as a youth, he spent all his time in a single robe to endure both cold and heat.
Once, while traveling with several senior monks through the region of Xiang’an,
there was a monk who was quite agile in discussing the *zongcheng* (the vehicle of the school).
We happened upon a mountain inn where a meal was being prepared for our wild-food lunch.
As the monks continued their discussion without ceasing, the Master said:
"The three realms are but mind; the myriad dharmas are but consciousness."
"Only consciousness, only mind; eye, sound, ear, and form—whose words are these?
A monk said:
Fayan spoke. The Master asked,
"What is its meaning?"
He said, "Because it is only mind, the faculties and objects do not reach one another;
because it is only consciousness, sounds and forms are nonetheless present.
The Master said:
"Are the tongue and flavors the faculty and its object?
He replied, "Yes.
The Master placed a stalk of vegetable in his mouth with chopsticks and spoke with his mouth full: "What do you mean by 'mutual entry'?"
Those sitting there were startled, and the monk was unable to answer.
The Master said,
"The pleasures of the journey do not mean one has finally arrived home."
To have one's views penetrate subtly does not constitute the Path of Seeing;
one must practice with genuine inquiry and realize with genuine awakening.
"King Yama does not fear much talk.
The monk bowed and withdrew.
Later, he returned to Changsha and lived in seclusion at Mount Heng in the San-sheng Zang (Treasury of Three Lives).
A wealthy and nobleman from Xiangyin came to visit Fuyan.
Upon entering the Master’s quarters, he observed that the Master’s countenance was serene and composed; a single almsbowl hung on the wall, and there were no other possessions beyond it.
Struck with deep admiration, he prostrated himself and requested:
"The Divine Cauldron is the place where our family has cultivated merit for generations, yet it has long lacked a master craftsman.
What do you think of my wish that you, Master, go there with me?
The Master smiled and gave his consent.
He immediately loaded his own horse with his master;
it was not until the tenth year that he finally established a monastic seat,
using a single dilapidated bed as the Dharma throne for preaching.
His taste for the simple and austere was beyond compare;
moreover, because both his virtue and years were so great, he was honored by all quarters like the ancient Zhaozhou.
A monk asked,
"How is it when all dharmas have not yet been heard?
The Master said:
"The wind whistles and the rain falls in torrents.
He asked, "What was it like after that?
The Master said:
"Very well," he said.
He asked, "What is it like before the fish-drum has sounded?
The Master replied:
He looked at the sky and looked at the ground.
[The monk] asked, "What is it like after the sound?
The Master said:
Holding his bowl, he ascended the hall.
A monk asked, "What is it like when the cold spring flows in the ancient ravine?
The Master said:
"This is not the place for the conduct of a patch-robed monk.
[The monk] asked, "What then is the place for the conduct of a patch-robed monk?
The Master said:
He did not see the ancient stream or the cold spring.
He asked, "What is it like when both hands offer [flowers] to the Hall?
The Master said:
"What is this? [The Master asked.
"When a student goes to a mountain of jewels and returns empty-handed, how is it?
The Master said:
On the thirtieth day of the twelfth month,
someone asked, "What is the master's family style?
The Master said:
When hungry, one does not choose one's food.
[A monk] asked, "What is the Master’s phrase for benefiting people?
The Master said:
While gathering firewood and selecting vegetables,
[the Master] asked, "Is it not simply this very thing?
The Teacher replied:
"You must be even more meticulous.
He asked, "What is it like when one brushes away the dust and sees the Buddha?
The Master said:
"The Buddha is also a defilement.
[The student] asked, "What is the livelihood of a man of the Way?
The Master said:
"I, this mountain monk, have never entered a schoolhouse since childhood.
The official pointed to a wooden fish and asked, "What is this?"
The Master said,
"How many drowsy people have been startled back to life?
The Official said, [I understand].
When [the monk] had not yet arrived there,
the Master said:
"Strike the mindless with the mindless."
Question: "What is the pure Dharma-body?
The Master said:
"Ash on the head and dust on the face."
[The monk] asked, "Why is it so?
The Master said,
"How can you blame me, this mountain monk?"
[The monk] asked, "I have not yet ascertained whether there is anything further beyond the Dharma-body or not.
The Master said, "There is.
[The monk] asked, "What is this matter that lies beyond?"
The Master said:
"The golden crown atop the head of Vairocana.
[The monk] asked: "Since the Bodhi tree originally does not exist, from where did you obtain this crown?"
The Master said,
"Would you call this 'attaining nothing'?
He asked, "When the Bodhisattva Dhṛtarāṣṭra repairs roads and the like, and when the Upādhyāya repairs bridges and the like, who is it that acts?"
The Master said,
"Later on, ask him:
'Before you met the former virtuous ones, what was it like?'"
The Master said,
"Whether walking east or walking west.
